title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles
book_title: From Dorm-Room Classifieds to Automated Eyewear Factories

epigraph.quote: Focus is not saying yes to the thing you've got to focus on. It means saying no to the hundred other good ideas.
epigraph.author: Steve Jobs

web_blocks.html: Every durable consumer franchise begins when a founder treats the first business plan as tuition. Peyush Bansal, Amit Chaudhary, Sumeet Kapahi, and Neha Bansal incorporated Valyoo Technologies in 2008 [1][15]. Bansal returned from Microsoft to launch SearchMyCampus.com, a student portal, before pivoting to niche e-commerce. In late 2010, the team launched Lenskart online with contact lenses to avoid frame-fitting friction [15]. Between 2011 and 2012, they also added WatchKart, BagKart, and JewelsKart [15].

By 2014, running four unrelated portals broke down on unit economics. Watches, bags, and jewelry faced brutal marketplace competition and high acquisition costs. Eyewear offered a rare anomaly: gross margins above 65% without middlemen, steady repeat demand, and a fragmented local optician base [3][10]. Management shut down WatchKart, BagKart, and JewelsKart to focus capital on Lenskart. They then made a bold bet for an internet startup: opening physical stores and building in-house manufacturing [3][15].

web_blocks.takeaway: Lenskart's 18-year arc is defined by three deliberate pivots: pruning non-core e-commerce in 2014, backwards-integrating into robotics and physical stores in 2016–2021, and using cross-border M&A (Owndays, Meller) plus public equity capital (2025 IPO) to build a pan-Asian and European eyewear platform.

web_blocks.html: The second inflection arrived between 2016 and 2021. Buying finished frames and lenses from third parties capped both quality and delivery speed. Traditional Indian optical orders passed through importers, distributors, local opticians, and external labs. That chain took five to seven days and piled up 3x to 5x markups. Lenskart bypassed it by building an automated lens plant in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, using Addverb robotics for surfacing, coating, and assembly [8]. This spine enabled the 'Home Eye Test' program and rapid store rollouts across Tier-1, Tier-2, and Tier-3 cities.

From FY2020 to FY2022, Lenskart operated in venture-backed expansion mode. Revenue rose from ₹900 crore in FY20 to ₹1,503 crore in FY22 [1]. Operating profit stayed negative (-₹32 crore in FY20, -₹47 crore in FY21, and -₹115 crore in FY22) as equity funded store rollouts [1]. Equity reserves swelled from ₹2,333 crore in March 2020 to ₹5,441 crore by March 2023. SoftBank Vision Fund, Kedaara Capital, Alpha Wave Global, Temasek, and ADIA led those private rounds [1][11].

In mid-2022, Lenskart acquired a controlling stake in Japanese eyewear chain Owndays for roughly $400 million in cash and stock [6]. Overnight, Lenskart gained a retail footprint across 13 Asian markets, including Japan, Singapore, Thailand, and Taiwan. Consolidated revenue jumped 152% in FY23 to ₹3,788 crore and 43% in FY24 to ₹5,428 crore [1][6]. The deal also reshaped the balance sheet. Fixed assets leaped from ₹649 crore in FY22 to ₹5,067 crore in FY23, while lease borrowings rose from ₹34 crore to ₹934 crore and ₹2,343 crore in FY24 [1].

The latest chapter unfolded in 2025 and 2026. In July 2025, Lenskart bought an 80% stake in Barcelona-based D2C brand Meller for roughly ₹407 crore [9]. In November 2025, Lenskart listed on the NSE and BSE via a ₹7,278.02 crore IPO (₹2,150 crore fresh issue; ₹5,128.02 crore OFS) [4]. FY26 revenue grew 32% to ₹8,814 crore, with ₹501 crore net profit. TTM revenue through September 2026 reached ₹10,383 crore (+41%), with ₹797 crore PAT [1].

web_blocks.title: Post-IPO Ownership Shift & Promoter Stake Forensics
paragraphs: Pre-IPO venture rounds left promoter group ownership at 17.52% as of September 2026 (down slightly from 17.57% in December 2025) [1][5]. Public float is heavily institutional.

From December 2025 to September 2026, FII ownership surged from 3.86% to 18.26% [5]. DII ownership climbed from 15.86% to 26.81% over the same period [5]. Combined institutional sponsorship above 45% absorbed post-IPO supply, though 17.52% promoter skin-in-the-game remains a governance watchpoint.

web_blocks.html: Operating leverage accelerated after the listing. FY26 revenue rose 32% to ₹8,814 crore, while operating profit jumped 80% to ₹1,754 crore (19.9% OPM) [1]. TTM operating profit reached ₹2,209 crore (21% OPM) [1]. With 603 net new stores added in FY26, Lenskart shifted from cash-burning startup to self-funding retail leader [1][3].

What stands out across Lenskart's 18-year timeline is capital discipline after 2014 [15]. Many consumer-internet peers chased horizontal categories and burned cash without building supply-chain assets. Lenskart instead poured private equity into automated lens grinding in Bhiwadi and omnichannel store rollouts [8]. By FY23, consolidated revenue jumped 152% to ₹3,788 crore after the Owndays acquisition [1][6]. By FY25, net profit turned positive at ₹297 crore [1]. By FY26, free cash flow hit ₹846 crore even while adding 603 net new stores [1][3]. That shift from cash-burning startup to cash-generating leader explains why institutional ownership crossed 45% within a year of listing [5].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand why Lenskart looks so different from a typical Indian consumer startup, you have to go back to 2014, when Peyush Bansal did something remarkably rare in venture-backed e-commerce: he killed three businesses that were already generating traffic. Back in 2008, when Bansal and his co-founders Amit Chaudhary, Sumeet Kapahi, and Neha Bansal incorporated Valyoo Technologies, they were experimenting with what the Indian internet would buy. By 2012, the company was juggling Lenskart, WatchKart, BagKart, and JewelsKart. On paper, diversifying across fashion accessories looked like smart cross-selling. In reality, it was bleeding focus and capital.

You and I have seen this movie many times in consumer tech: a founder spreads engineering, marketing, and inventory across four unrelated categories, only to discover that horizontal marketplaces will always out-discount them on standardized goods. In 2014, Bansal shut down WatchKart, BagKart, and JewelsKart to bet the entire company on prescription eyewear. Why eyewear? Because a pair of prescription glasses is never a commodity. It is a medical device disguised as a fashion accessory, requiring an eye exam, precise lens surfacing, custom edging, and physical fitting. That complexity kept Amazon and Flipkart at bay while leaving traditional neighborhood opticians vulnerable to anyone who could automate the back-end lab.

That realization triggered Lenskart's second great pivot: moving out of the browser and into concrete and steel. Between 2015 and 2021, Lenskart built an automated manufacturing and lens-processing hub in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, equipping it with robotics that could cut, coat, and assemble custom prescription glasses at industrial scale. At the same time, it began opening physical stores across India—first in metro malls and high streets, then deep into Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns—linking online browsing, home eye tests, and store pick-up into a single inventory pool. While pure-play online rivals struggled with return rates and customer trust, Lenskart turned physical stores into high-converting customer acquisition engines.

What makes Lenskart's corporate evolution especially instructive is that it never relied on a single lucky break. First came the 2014 focus pivot; then came the Bhiwadi automated manufacturing bet that turned custom prescription glasses into a 24-to-72-hour fulfillment cycle; then came the 2022 Owndays acquisition that gave Lenskart instant scale across thirteen Asian markets; and finally came the 2025 Meller acquisition and NSE/BSE listing that fortified its balance sheet with ₹9,322 Cr of shareholders' equity. Every milestone compounded the underlying supply-chain advantage rather than diluting it.

book_subsections.title: The Cross-Border Leap: Owndays, Meller, and the 2025 IPO
paragraphs: By 2022, Lenskart had proved the omnichannel model in India, scaling revenue from ₹900 crore in FY20 to ₹1,503 crore in FY22, though it was still reporting operating losses as it plowed cash into store rollouts. Rather than staying purely domestic, management made an audacious move in mid-2022, acquiring a controlling stake in Japan's Owndays in a roughly $400 million stock-and-cash deal. Overnight, Lenskart inherited a respected retail brand across 13 Asian markets—including Japan, Singapore, Thailand, Taiwan, and the Philippines—and jumped consolidated revenue by 152% to ₹3,788 crore in FY23.

In July 2025, Lenskart repeated that playbook in Europe, paying roughly ₹407 crore for an 80% stake in Meller, a Barcelona-born digital-native sunglasses brand favored by younger European and American shoppers. Four months later, in November 2025, Lenskart listed on the NSE and BSE in a ₹7,278 crore IPO. Crucially, only ₹2,150 crore of that offering was fresh capital for new stores and technology; the remaining ₹5,128 crore was an Offer for Sale allowing early venture backers to take partial exits. That capital history explains why founder-promoter ownership sits at 17.52% today—a structure more akin to a widely held global tech-retailer than a traditional family-controlled Indian conglomerate.

book_subsections.title: From Valyoo Technologies to a ₹10,383 Cr Omnichannel Giant: The Financial Arc
paragraphs: To appreciate how unusual Lenskart's trajectory is, walk through the numbers year by year with me. In FY20, Lenskart was still a ₹900 Cr private startup navigating the pandemic's lockdown shock, when online eye-testing and home try-on kits kept the business alive while mall stores went dark. By FY22, revenue had climbed to ₹1,503 Cr, but heavy store rollouts and brand-building pushed operating profit margins down to minus 8%, with an operating loss of ₹116 Cr.

Then came the inflection. In mid-2022, Lenskart acquired a majority stake in Japan's Owndays in a roughly $400 million stock-and-cash transaction, instantly inheriting a profitable footprint across 13 Asian markets including Japan, Singapore, Taiwan, and Thailand. Consolidated revenue surged 152% in FY23 to ₹3,788 Cr, and operating profit swung positive to ₹264 Cr (a 7% margin), even as net profit remained negative at minus ₹64 Cr due to ₹418 Cr of Ind AS 116 depreciation and amortization.

From FY24 through FY26, scale economics took over. Revenue rose 43% in FY24 to ₹5,428 Cr (OPM 13%, ₹680 Cr operating profit), grew 23% in FY25 to ₹6,653 Cr (OPM 15%, ₹977 Cr operating profit, and first full-year net profit of ₹297 Cr), and accelerated 32% in FY26 to ₹8,814 Cr (OPM 19.9%, ₹1,754 Cr operating profit, ₹501 Cr net profit). Along the way, Lenskart acquired an 80% stake in European D2C eyewear brand Meller in July 2025 for roughly ₹407 Cr, completed its ₹7,278.02 Cr IPO in November 2025 (comprising ₹2,150 Cr of fresh primary capital and ₹5,128.02 Cr of secondary OFS), and pushed trailing twelve-month revenue through September 2026 to ₹10,383 Cr with ₹797 Cr in net profit. Across those six years, FIIs and DIIs stepped in to lift combined institutional ownership above 45%, while promoter holding settled at 17.52%.

book_subsections.title: Why the 2014 Pivot Still Defines Lenskart's Culture
paragraphs: Before we move to Lenskart's product segments, pause for a moment on that 2014 decision to shut down WatchKart, BagKart, and JewelsKart. Most Indian consumer-internet founders of that era chased horizontal GMV across as many categories as venture capital would subsidize. Peyush Bansal, Amit Chaudhary, and Sumeet Kapahi realized that eyewear was fundamentally different: it combined high gross margins (~65% to 70%) with a technical medical barrier—precision lens grinding and optometry—that horizontal marketplaces like Amazon or Flipkart could never commoditize.

That single strategic choice—owning the entire stack from frame design to automated lens edging and in-store eye exams—explains why Lenskart survived the 2016–2019 e-commerce funding winter, thrived through the 2020 pandemic, and emerged as a ₹10,383 Cr revenue leader by 2026. Every subsequent move, from Bhiwadi's robotics to Owndays' 13-country footprint and the November 2025 IPO, is a direct extension of that 2014 vertical-integration thesis.

book_subsections.title: The Institutionalization of India's Eyewear Leader
paragraphs: Look at how the shareholder register evolved immediately after the November 2025 listing. At ₹7,278.02 Cr, the IPO was one of India's most closely watched consumer-tech offerings, combining ₹2,150 Cr of fresh growth capital with ₹5,128.02 Cr of early-investor exits. Within three quarters, Foreign Institutional Investors raised their stake from 3.86% in December 2025 to 18.26% by September 2026, while Domestic Institutional Investors nearly doubled their holding from 15.86% to 26.81%.

That rapid institutionalization stabilized the balance sheet—pushing net worth to ₹9,322 Cr—and gave Lenskart the financial firepower to fund its ₹1,500 Cr Hyderabad mega-facility without taking on heavy bank debt.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Killing Three Businesses Created One Moat
book_callouts.text: When we study compounding businesses together, we often obsess over what management launched. With Lenskart, the decisive moment was what management killed. Shutting down WatchKart, BagKart, and JewelsKart in 2014 freed the team to build robotic lens labs in Bhiwadi and a 3,300-store global network. Yet the same venture-funded speed that built that scale also left behind a 17.52% promoter stake and a multi-country integration puzzle. As we move into the business segments and unit economics, keep asking yourself: is the international expansion amplifying the Indian factory moat, or diluting its capital efficiency?
